title: The phantom city (Kern ch. 7)
hook: a guide conjures a city so tired travelers can rest, then says the treasure is further on
tomorrow: The jewel in the coat (Kern ch. 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long story of a past Buddha, whose sixteen sons taught the Lotus, the sixteenth being the Buddha himself. Your line: sixteen sons. Did you thank someone in your chain of teachers? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

Halfway up a hard trail, the group has stopped talking. Legs are shaking. Someone says what everyone is thinking: let's just go back down. And the trip leader, who has walked this trail many times, says: there's a hut just past the next bend. Water, shade, a place to sit. They make it to the hut. They rest. And later, rested, they find the summit was closer than they thought. Chapter seven of the Lotus ends with a guide like that, though his hut is something stranger. Today: the phantom city.
screen: `LEGS SHAKING, HALFWAY UP.` → `LET'S JUST GO BACK.` → `A HUT PAST THE NEXT BEND.`

segments.voice: First, the wilderness. In Kern's translation the Buddha tells of a great crowd setting out across a wild and fearful forest, on a long road, to reach a place of treasure. Their guide is wise and knows every turn of the way. But partway along the travelers are worn out and frightened. We can't go on, they say. It's too far. Let's turn back. Second, the city. The guide doesn't scold them. He is skilled in means, the sutra says, and he feels for them. So, by his own power, he makes a city appear in the middle of the wilderness. Look, he says, here is a city. Go in and rest. The travelers are delighted. They go in, they rest, they feel safe, and they think they have arrived. Third, the disappearing. When the guide sees they are rested, he makes the city vanish. Then he tells them: that city was something I made for you to rest in. The treasure is near. Come, let's go on. Fourth, the meaning. The Buddha explains. He is the guide, and the road is long and hard. If beings heard only about the far goal, Buddhahood, many would lose heart and turn back. So he teaches a resting place along the way: the peace, the release, the disciples have reached. It is real rest, and it is given out of care. But it is not the end. The treasure, the Buddha's own awakening, is further on. Look at what the city is not. It isn't a trick to punish anyone, or a test. It's there because tired people need somewhere to sit down. And the guide stays with them the whole way. Over the last days the sutra has given us carts, a dirt heap, rain. Here the same idea comes as shelter: rest is part of the road.
screen: `A LONG ROAD, TIRED TRAVELERS.` · `A CITY MADE TO REST IN.` · `THE CITY VANISHES.` · `THE TREASURE IS FURTHER ON.` · then, large: `A CITY TO REST IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: rest, then go on. For the first part of the sit, rest completely. Let the shoulders drop, the jaw loosen, the hands go heavy. Nowhere to get to. Breathe. Let this moment be the city in the wilderness. Then, toward the end, gently bring to mind one thing that's waiting for you today, a task or a conversation. Don't rush at it. Just turn toward it, rested, the way the travelers turned back to the road. The bell holds the time.

The phantom city. In chapter seven, a guide conjures a city so worn-out travelers can rest, then tells them the treasure lies further on: a resting place given out of care, on the way to the real goal. Today's word.
Your line: a city to rest in. Today, when you're tired partway through something, take a real rest without quitting, then pick it back up. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The parable of the conjured city, which closes chapter seven of the Lotus Sutra, is taught in East Asian Buddhism as a picture of skillful means: the rest of the disciples' release is real, offered out of compassion, and the road goes on to Buddhahood.

fork.setup: you are the guide. your travelers are exhausted and frightened, and they want to turn back. the treasure is still far. what do you do?
options: tell them the full distance so they know
make a city appear so they can rest
leave them and go on alone
fork.reveal: he conjures a city in the wilderness; when they are rested, he makes it vanish and tells them the treasure is near.

original.note: Sanskrit: city, town; in chapter seven, a city the guide makes appear in the wilderness.

trapdoor: what you thought: the guide tricked them with a fake city.
what it means: the guide gave real rest to worn-out travelers, then told them the truth: the treasure is further on.

what a scholar hears: the city stands for the disciples' nirvana as a resting stage; like the carts of chapter three, it is upaya, and the parable closes chapter seven's account of the Buddha's long care for his hearers.

notes: Chapter 7 closing parable paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted.
